explanation: `git init` creates the `.git` directory and starts tracking the folder.
tip: Only run `git init` once per project root.

explanation: All commit objects, tree snapshots, and branch pointers live inside `.git`.
tip: Deleting `.git` removes all version history but leaves your raw files intact.
Think of staging as packing a box, and commit as sealing and shipping it.

explanation: `git status` is your most frequently used command. When in doubt, run `git status`.
tip: Use `git status -s` for a compact, short view.

explanation: `git add` copies changes into the index (staging area).
tip: You can stage parts of a file interactively using `git add -p`.

explanation: `git add .` is convenient, but make sure you don't stage unwanted files like passwords or binaries.
tip: Always check `git status` after `git add .` to see what got staged.

explanation: Without `-m`, Git opens your configured terminal editor (Vim/nano/VS Code).
tip: Write commit messages in imperative mood: 'Add feature' rather than 'Added feature'.

explanation: Untracked files are invisible to Git's snapshot history until `git add` is used.
tip: Files listed in `.gitignore` will not even show up as untracked.

explanation: Staging enables atomic commits: bug fix in one commit, styling in another.
tip: Atomic commits make reading history and reverting bugs effortless.

explanation: `git commit -am` skips `git add` for modified tracked files only.
tip: If a new file won't commit with `-am`, check if it's untracked!
